entries.body: One week in Port Antonio — it was enough, even though the beer was cold, the fresh food delicious, the surroundings lush. The place has become very run down. Only a few boats in the harbor. We took a raft trip on the Rio Grande river — poled on a bamboo raft. It was nice to see the countryside. It is a good harbor — we weren't quite ready for the waves and swells outside. Beat to windward in 10–15 knots along the coast — kind of bumpy. Will bear off when we pass Morant Point. Charlotte is flying! The akee and breadfruit we had for dinner last night was excellent, along with Dragon Stout. Bound for the San Blas Islands.
entries.conditions: After one week in Port Antonio, Jamaica. Wind: 10–15 knots, beating to windward along the coast.

entries.body: Since we had forgotten, we got a rude reminder of the Caribbean wind and seas! Nice sailing last night — beautiful stars, broad reach in 15 knots, until we went under the squall line. Then bam — wind turned ESE, picked up to 25–30, and stayed there all day. Down to reefed mizzen and deeply reefed genoa. Not what we had hoped for. All we can do is lie around and try to eat. Brian won't leave the aft cabin. The sea is pretty though, with all the foaming waves. When the boat goes over 7–7.5 knots, the motion gets violent and we have to shorten sail.
entries.conditions: Wind: turned ESE, 25–30 knots. Reefed mizzen and deeply reefed genoa.

entries.body: It's rough, you can't be outside without taking a shower. Beautiful sunny weather though! Speed 4.5–5.5 knots, with same sail — reefed mizzen and reefed genoa. Can't do anything. Brian is feeling better today, still not eating much. The clew lines broke today.
entries.conditions: Speed 4.5–5.5 knots. Reefed mizzen and reefed genoa.

entries.body: [Even] more wind this morning — 30–35 knots, big seas. Since we [only] have 200 miles to go, we decided to slow the boat down so we arrive Tuesday morning. Reefed the genoa down to handkerchief size and put a second reef in the mizzen. Still taking occasional breakers over the boat. It's impossible to be on deck without getting soaked. There is nothing to do but lie around. Sailing is so much fun!
entries.conditions: Wind: 30–35 knots, big seas. Genoa reefed to handkerchief size, second reef in mizzen. 200 miles to go.

entries.body: A nicer day altogether! The wind turned NE last night so we are off the wind. Brian is his usual self again! It's down to 20+ today — sailing along with the same tiny sail rig at 4 knots so we will arrive at San Blas tomorrow after sunrise. We were able to be on deck today and enjoy the fresh air. Took a big breaker into the boat this morning — soaked the chart table — got to do something about that. We have learned a lot about Charlotte and sailing in wind on this trip, although the lesson has been uncomfortable!
entries.conditions: Wind: NE, 20+ knots, off the wind. 4 knots under reduced rig.

entries.body: Beautiful landfall, after a long uncomfortable rolly night. We saw a lot of ships at one point, must have been crossing the Canal shipping lane. Finally hoisted the main again as we approached Holandes Cays. Decided that weather cloths will help keep water out of the boat. It's beautiful here — our first landfall in a new place — finally breaking new ground with Charlotte! It is very sunny and the sun is hot. Water is all colors of blue — islands covered with palm trees. 550 mile sail — 4½ days.
entries.conditions: Landfall at Holandes Cays. 550-mile passage in 4½ days.

entries.body: Enjoyed our stay in the San Blas islands — anchored at Holandes Cays, Green Island, and Chichimé. Good windsurfing at Green Island. Bought some molas, enjoyed the Kuna Indians — very gentle and friendly. They had very nice dugouts, sailed some of them. The islands were green, palm-covered, the water blue like the Bahamas, beautiful reefs, but very few fish. Met the Austrian boat Idemo with Robert, Ingrid and 5-yr Anna aboard. Had some pleasant day sails around the islands. The weather was overcast — more towards the mainland. On the outer islands, the reefs crashed constantly and everything was salty.
entries.conditions: About 11 days in the San Blas, anchoring at Holandes Cays, Green Island, and Chichimé.

entries.body: Left early this morning for Portobelo. 3 other boats left too. It was a superhighway along Panama's north coast! Boisterous sailing, 20–25 knots, beam reach, reefed genoa, reefed mizzen, double-reefed main. We kept up pretty well with the bigger boats. Finally got to see the green hills of the Panama coast towards the end of the trip. Coast is rocky, mostly deep to shore, but with numerous off-lying reefs. Not a place to sail at night! Portobelo is a beautiful natural harbor — plenty big for a fleet of Spanish galleons! 55 miles in 8½ hours, over 6½ knots average.
entries.conditions: Wind: 20–25 knots, beam reach. Reefed genoa, reefed mizzen, double-reefed main. 55 miles in 8½ hours, 6½ knot average.

entries.body: Downwind sail to Colón today — nice sail for a change, no waves on deck! The coastline is green and rugged. Entering the breakwater at Colón was exciting. Big nasty town. We loved Portobelo — most beautiful anchorage we have ever seen. Three forts guarding the entrance from all sides. We climbed to the top of one fort, took a short dinghy ride up a river. Peter's boat Tiamat was there — we met him in Brazil — but he had died two weeks before. We enjoyed the little town, felt comfortable standing around drinking beer. Now the real hustle begins.
entries.conditions: Downwind sail to Colón.

entries.body: Well our stay in Colón was a lot more fun than we expected. It helped that we met some people! In particular, Kelcey, Jim, Chris, and Nicholas who is Brian's age. He was off at the yacht club every afternoon, so Thomas and I had a lot of time alone together, which was very nice. They bought a new outboard motor — 4 HP Yamaha. We enjoyed the street food of Colón, although it was a filthy city. Must have been nice at one point — many sidewalks were tiled, indications of past glory. It was easy to get around though, and people were friendly and helpful, proud to have our business for the most part. Transited the canal today, rafted to a French boat [Jonaia]. We had 3 American line handlers on board — only Ken, the boat owner, knew what he was doing. It was all right when the [French] boat was steering us along the tugs, as their pilot was complet[ely] [illegible]. But when Thomas had to do the steering, the wind and current rammed [us] into the side wall. Broke the stanchion Don had welded, scraped the side but no paint lost. We roared through Lake Gatún under motor and genoa, going as fast as we were able. It was very interesting, sailing through the middle of Panama! Had a wait a long time at the last locks, so we didn't clear them until after 6. It was 8 pm, completely dark, by the time we anchored at Flamenco Cay. What an experience! No need to repeat it soon.
entries.conditions: About two weeks in Colón. Transited the Panama Canal — Caribbean side to Pacific side. Anchored at Flamenco after dark.

entries.body: Finally leaving the Panama Canal Zone! Left this morning from Flamenco Cay anchorage for Las Perlas. Light wind, but pleasant sailing at 3–4 knots, full sails, no rolling! After 3 weeks of rolling with pilot boat wakes, it is a pleasure. Panama City was BIG! Buses were confusing, taxis comfortable but more expensive. We got what we needed there — speargun, spare parts, more food and booze. I had my loose tooth pulled. The usual assortment of older Americans and European single-handers. Wind picked up later in the morning and we had a great sail in calm — Pacific! — waters, through the islands, to Contadora. Reef anchorage — 40 feet.
entries.conditions: About one week at Flamenco / Panama City. Wind light, 3–4 knots, full sails. Anchored at Contadora in 40 feet.

entries.body: Well Las Perlas was not exactly what we expected. Contadora was rolly and uncomfortable, so we moved 15 miles to Viveros Cay. Pretty anchorage, surrounded by beaches and little islands, but the murky water was disappointing — spearfishing out of the question. Then Thomas stepped on something in the shallow water and got the most horrific infection. He was in pain, couldn't walk for 3 days, and his foot kept getting worse. Meanwhile Brian and I enjoyed walks on the beaches at low tide and had fun scrambling around on the rocks. The shells were mostly scallops, purple and orange. Beautiful views across the islands from some shady rock under a tree. I really enjoyed the solitude there — no one but small local fishing boats, gorgeous skies at night. We finally went back to Contadora on Thurs Mar. 7 and luckily there was a doctor there. Thomas was in for 5 days of shots, heavy anti[biotics], and his foot slowly started to heal. Very nice young doctor — Cresmo [Garcia], who was interested in our plans and gave us some [medication] to take with us. We got used to touristy Contadora — really just a sleepy town — and had our routine of afternoon ice cream and beer at the local mini super. Very dry though — no water — I now wash what I can in sea water. We enjoyed our waiting time as best [we] could.
entries.conditions: About two weeks in the Las Perlas, between Contadora and Isla Viveros, including Thomas's foot infection and treatment.

entries.body: Now Thomas is almost completely healed and we are under way for the Galápagos! Left this morning, after a favorable wind report from boats on the way. We have been sailing past the Perlas all day, under full genoa and then spinnaker. 12 knots wind NNE, tiny seas, beautiful sailing, the boat is upright! Good omen this morning — we saw a perfect rainbow circle around the sun. Panama was a pleasant surprise, really enjoyed the scenery, the friendly people, the great food, the cheap beer! Could have stayed longer if that was our plan. For now, we are happy to be underway again, with a fair wind. The Pacific truly lives up to its name, at least at these latitudes!
entries.conditions: Departing Las Perlas for the Galápagos. Wind: NNE, 12 knots, tiny seas. Full genoa, then spinnaker.

entries.body: Here we are, cruising along at 5.5 knots, under spinnaker and mizzen. Thomas is happy — no sail chafe, and he has always wanted to fly the mizzen drifter since it is so weird. It works great on a broad reach. Winds just turned more easterly and are filling in 6–8 knots. Last night we had an incredible ride — 8.5, surfing to [past] [illegible] for several hours in 20+ knots, broad reaching. The boat was [so] [illegible] it was almost scary, but the [Aries] steered well. The wind died down this morning for a while. All in all it has been very pleasant. [Lots] of sea life, not sure what we are seeing.
entries.conditions: Wind: easterly, 6–8 knots. Spinnaker and mizzen. First 24-hour run — 148 miles.

entries.body: Ran under our funny rig until the middle of the night when the wind picked up. NE winds, 15–20, full sail, boomed out genoa, 5+ knots. Got a bit rolly for a while. Weather report is favorable, some wind tomorrow. All happy on board.
entries.conditions: Wind: NE, 15–20 knots. Full sail, boomed-out genoa, 5+ knots. 24-hour run — 117 miles.

entries.body: Well so much for weather reports! Very light wind last night, banged and rolled, down to 2 knots. More of same today, slightly more wind. Spinnaker flying. It is comfortable when we don't roll — hardly know we are at sea. We are well rested, nothing going on at night. Put a spreader chafe patch on the main sail this morning.
entries.conditions: Wind: very light, down to 2 knots. Spinnaker flying. 24-hour run — 106 miles.

entries.body: Another slow night, averaged 3.5 knots, but wind came up some in the morning. Now it is dying again. At least we continue to move! Spent the day working on a crew list in 3 languages. Brian is getting adept at the computer. The water is blue here, and we must have some current.
entries.conditions: Averaged 3.5 knots. 24-hour run — 97 miles.

entries.body: It got worse. Totally becalmed for hours last night — we just slept. Wind came up at 3 am from the south so we took down the pole. 3–4 knots in 6 knots of wind — amazing Charlotte can move at all! Now we are motoring because Thomas is impatient. It's really horrible.
entries.conditions: Becalmed, then 3–4 knots in 6 knots of wind from the south. Motoring. 24-hour run — 75 miles.

entries.body: Three 24-hour run — [80] m — nothing more needs to be said. Can you believe — head winds! We alternate between sailing south or west and motoring. Big swell from the SW hampers our progress. Kind of frustrating.
entries.conditions: Head winds; alternating sailing and motoring. Big SW swell. 24-hour run — 87 miles.

entries.body: Landfall this morning at sunrise! We motored all night in calm [seas]. It was a bummer, but we're here and San Cristóbal is beautiful. Dolphins playing, sea lions on the beaches, huge eagle rays lying on the surface, looking like sharks with double fins. Kicker Rock looks like a big foot. We dropped anchor in Wreck Bay around 11, a number of boats we saw in Panama are here. Everyone is friendly.
entries.conditions: Landfall at Puerto Baquerizo Moreno (Wreck Bay) at sunrise. Motored all night in calm seas.

entries.body: It has been a fun 10 days in Puerto Baquerizo Moreno — we really enjoyed the town and harbor. The sea lions were constant entertainment, swimming and playing around the boats, climbing up on every possible surface. We had to pick up the dinghy every night or they would have sunk it. We went on a land tour to El Junco and around with the Dutch boat Kenza and the [Danish-Brazilian] Sundowner II. Our taxi driver Carlos took us to a friend's [farm] where we picked fresh fruits and vegetables in the pouring [rain], using banana leaves over our heads like umbrellas. It was the highlight of the day — so peaceful in the fields, with the [illegible] singing and a view of the east coast of the island. We drank cheap beer at a panadería and got to know all the local shopkeepers. Made friends with Steve & Sharon on Poet's Place and [flying] genoa on Candlewin. Visited the Interpretive Center and learned about the history of the Galápagos. We saw blue-footed boobies [diving] for fish behind the boat, lava lizards and marine iguanas basking in the sun on the lava rocks, very prehistoric looking. We were amazed [at] the lushness of the island — everything grows in the rich volcanic soil.
entries.conditions: About 11 days at San Cristóbal. Land tour to El Junco; visited the Interpretive Center.

entries.body: Weird night, drifting west with the current. Motored at sunrise, just went to get there. Went close to Isla Tortuga, sunken volcano crater, half moon out of water, cool to look at! Puerto Villamil at Isabela is beautiful, tucked between some lava islands and the shore, with sandy beaches and palm trees. The little islands contain all kinds of wild life — Galápagos penguins, small, black & white, very awkward and funny on land, blue-footed boobies with their unbelievable bright blue feet, marine iguanas looking like prehistoric monsters, and of course sea lions! There is a turtle hatchery a short walk away and a lagoon full of pink flamingos. Fascinating! Plus lots of boats, parties on the beach. We love it here!
entries.conditions: Drifting and motoring to Isabela. Anchored at Puerto Villamil.

entries.body: Left Puerto Villamil yesterday afternoon, after a false start. We were chased by the Port Captain and asked to return and check out properly! No big deal — he is really a nice guy. Hard to describe the wonderful time we had at Isabela. Athanor showed up with Beeca, 10 and Ollie 8, and their parents Eddie and Eileen. All the boats from Wreck Bay eventually pulled in. Attended a wild party at Jeff & Claudia's house, American and Argentinian living here with their kids. Saw all kinds of wild life. Went to the turtle hatchery and saw turtles from 1 month to 100 years old. Found a lagoon full of pink flamingos. Took a great horseback ride to the volcano — it was really neat, riding up the outside of the mountain, then walking on the lava fields down into the crater. It was like a moonscape — mostly black but other colors when the sun shone on it. Some deep clefts were still smoking, ferns growing in them. This one had erupted in 1969. We passed another crater on horseback that is the second largest volcanic crater in the world. Very interesting day. Brian went again, with the other kids. He had such a good time, playing all day on the beach. We barely saw him! One day we went dinghying with Jean and Sherry on Reflection, helped a sick tortoise that was covered with oysters. I thought he was dead at first. Brian and I saw him again 2 days later, swimming normally and able to dive. We got very close to some penguins. Another day I actually touched one that was sitting on a rock! They were all standing there, stretching their stubby wings, wearing their black and white tuxedos! Brian and I went on an early morning walk on the lava islands and saw hundreds of iguanas, almost stepped on them. Got into a routine of walking to town at 4 pm for a delicious homemade pastry fresh from the bakery and an ice cold beer. Decided not to go to Easter Island with Greg & genoa on Candlewin — we need to stay with Athanor for Brian. We will miss those guys though. It was hard to leave Isabela, with the incredible wildlife and the renewed social life. But I was rewarded with the sight of a school of 100 dolphins yesterday before dark. They were leaping 10 feet out of the water — amazing — so many at once! Had a squall last night, good wind, then it was light, did 3 knots. Now we are motoring for a few hours to try to get into the wind. Galápagos, we love you!
entries.conditions: About 12 days at Isabela. Departed for the Marquesas. 24-hour run — 89 miles.
